title: Backup and Restore
summary: Back up MySQL with mysqldump and MySQL Shell's dump utilities, restore and verify a database, understand logical versus physical backups and use binary logs for point-in-time recovery.
introduction: A database you cannot restore is a database you do not have. Disks fail, but far more often someone runs DELETE without a WHERE or a migration goes wrong, and the only fix is a copy from before the mistake. This lesson shows the two logical backup tools that ship with MySQL, how to restore and verify a dump, what the binary log adds, and when a physical backup tool is the better choice. The commands run in a terminal, not inside the mysql client.
learningObjectives: Create a consistent logical backup of one or all databases with mysqldump
Restore a dump into a new database and verify it
Use MySQL Shell's dumpSchemas and loadDump utilities for large databases
Explain binary logs, point-in-time recovery and physical backups

blocks.text: A *logical* backup is a set of SQL statements or data files that recreate the database by running them; a *physical* backup is a copy of InnoDB's own data files. Logical backups are portable across versions and platforms and easy to inspect; physical backups are much faster to take and restore for large databases.

rows: Databases up to tens of gigabytes, version upgrades, copying a schema to another server
MySQL Enterprise Backup (commercial), Percona XtraBackup (free), the Clone plugin, storage snapshots
Large databases, fast full restores, building replicas

blocks.text: `mysqlpump`, a parallel alternative to `mysqldump`, was deprecated in 8.0.34 and removed in 8.4; MySQL Shell's utilities replace it.

`mysqldump` connects like any client and writes `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT` statements to standard output, so redirect it into a file. `--single-transaction` takes a consistent InnoDB snapshot without locking the tables; `--routines`, `--triggers` and `--events` include stored programs, which are otherwise left out. The first lines of the file identify the server that produced it.

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.code:
mysqldump --single-transaction --routines --triggers --events \
  -u root -p roastery > roastery.sql

head -n 5 roastery.sql

blocks.content:
Enter password:
-- MySQL dump 10.13  Distrib 8.4.6, for Linux (x86_64)
--
-- Host: localhost    Database: roastery
-- ------------------------------------------------------
-- Server version	8.4.6

rows: Every database on the server, including the `mysql` system database with its accounts
Named databases, with `CREATE DATABASE` and `USE` statements included so the restore recreates them
Writes the file directly, which avoids line-ending surprises in PowerShell
Adds the binary log position of the snapshot as a comment, for point-in-time recovery or setting up a replica
Omits GTID information when the dump will be loaded into an unrelated server

blocks.title: Without --single-transaction the dump blocks writers and may be inconsistent
blocks.text: By default `mysqldump` locks each table while reading it, so a dump taken during business hours stalls the application, and tables dumped at different moments can disagree with each other: an order referencing a customer who was inserted after `customers` was dumped. Always add `--single-transaction` for InnoDB. MyISAM tables cannot be snapshotted and need `--lock-all-tables` instead.

A dump is restored by feeding it to the `mysql` client. Restoring into a fresh database lets you verify the result before touching the real one; then rename or point the application at it. `-e` runs a single statement and exits, printing the result in table form.

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.code:
mysql -u root -p -e "CREATE DATABASE roastery_restore"
mysql -u root -p roastery_restore < roastery.sql
mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders FROM roastery_restore.orders"

blocks.content:
Enter password:
Enter password:
Enter password:
+--------+
| orders |
+--------+
|      8 |
+--------+

blocks.text: Inside the client, `source roastery.sql` does the same as the redirect. Large restores are faster with `SET autocommit = 0` and `SET unique_checks = 0` at the top of the session and a single `COMMIT` at the end; the dump already wraps each table's inserts this way. If you only need one table, dump it alone with `mysqldump roastery orders`.

MySQL Shell (`mysqlsh`) dumps in parallel, compresses on the fly and splits large tables into chunks, so it is the tool for databases that take `mysqldump` hours. `util.dumpSchemas` and `util.dumpInstance` write a directory; `util.loadDump` reads it back, can resume after an interruption and needs `local_infile` enabled on the target server (`SET GLOBAL local_infile = ON;`).

blocks.text: Since 8.0 the server keeps a *binary log* by default: an append-only record of every change, used for replication and for recovery. A nightly dump plus the binary logs since that dump lets you restore the database to any second, including the one *before* a destructive statement. `SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS` is the 8.2 and later name of the old `SHOW MASTER STATUS`, which 8.4 no longer accepts.

blocks.code:
SHOW BINARY LOGS;

SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS;

blocks.text: File names, sizes and positions are specific to your server. To recover, restore the last dump, then replay the log from the position recorded by `--source-data` up to just before the bad statement; `mysqlbinlog` converts the binary format into SQL that the client can execute.
Binary logs are purged after `binlog_expire_logs_seconds` (30 days by default); keep that longer than the interval between full backups, or the chain has a gap.
Physical backups and the rules that matter

When a logical dump takes too long, copy the files instead. MySQL Enterprise Backup and Percona XtraBackup copy InnoDB data while the server runs and record the log position; the Clone plugin (`CLONE INSTANCE FROM ...`, 8.0.17 and later) copies a whole running server to another, which is the fastest way to build a replica. A file-system snapshot works only if the server is stopped or the data is flushed and locked first.

items: Schedule backups and keep at least one copy off the server, ideally off-site.
Test a restore on a schedule: a backup that has never been restored is an assumption.
Record how long the backup and the restore take; that number is your recovery time.
Protect dump files as you protect the database: they contain every row and, with `--all-databases`, every password hash.
Back up accounts too: either `--all-databases` or a separate dump of the `mysql` database.

questions.question: How do you restore `roastery.sql` into the database `roastery_restore`?
questions.explanation: A dump is plain SQL, so the mysql client executes it. mysqldump only writes dumps; it does not read them.

questions.question: With a nightly mysqldump and the binary logs since that dump, you can restore the database to the moment just before a bad DELETE.
questions.explanation: That is point-in-time recovery: restore the dump, then replay the binary log with mysqlbinlog up to the statement you want to exclude.
